newsitem.title: UK: Dollar sails to 1.51 marks on wave of buying.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sails to 1.51 marks on wave of buying.

text.p: The dollar raced to 1.51 marks and 110 yen in afternoon Europe on Tuesday as the U.S. currency finally pierced through key technical barriers.
U.S. funds climbed in to trigger stop-loss dollar buying near 1.5050/60 marks, while comments by Federal Reserve official offered fundamental support, dealers and analysts said.
The break of 1.5050/60 marks and 1.2300 Swiss francs were the initial technical catalysts as both were key 50 retracements of the dollar's May to July decline, analysts said.
The dollar was stalling just below 1.51 marks by 1600 GMT, still nearly two pfennigs above late Monday's 1.4910 close.
"Once we moved beyond 1.50, it's momentum-driven," said Keld Holm, international economist at Lehman Brothers.
Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke spooked dollar bulls out of hiding yesterday when he said that there was room for further German interest rate cuts if M3 growth continues to slow.

Prospects of widening U.S.-German interest rate differentials intensified this afternoon after Federal Reserve governor Janet Yellen said in a Reuters interview the U.S. economy has entered an inflationary danger zone and that the Fed must be alert to the risk that could pose to continued economic expansion.
The dollar is now trading above levels seen on July 16, when dollar/mark suffered its biggest one-day drop this year as New York share prices crashed.
The dollar rallied to 1.2332 Swiss francs by 1554 GMT, sharply above a 1.2157 close in Europe late yesterday.

Jiro Nagato, senior dealer at Sumitomo Bank in London, said the dollar's move in Europe was ignited in dollar/Swiss after the Swiss National Bank was seen to have injected ample liquidity into the money market this morning.
Although current Swiss franc weakness is attributed more to dollar strength, economists said the Swiss unit was long overdue for a period of independent weakness given its weak economy.
In other dollar pairs, the dollar surpassed 109.45 resistance and was within grasp of the 110 target by 1542 GMT versus Monday's 109.07.

The high-yielding lira continued to benefit from overall mark lethargy as talk of the lira's return to the ERM at 1,000 bubbled. It rose to 1006.40 per mark at 1555 GMT versus 1011.00/35 late on Monday.
Focus is glued on the U.S. Federal Reserve and a possible credit-tightening as the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on September 24 approaches.

Speculation is intensifying ahead of the Beige Book, the Fed's account of its view of the U.S. economy, Wednesday and producer and consumer prices on Thursday and Friday respectively. Retail sales data are also due on Friday.

Lehman's Holm also said there was a possibility that the Fed may raise the federal funds target rate by 25 basis points from the current 5.25 percent soon because raising interest rates a day before the U.S. presidential debate begins on September 25 was likely to ruffle political feathers.
Despite the anxiety over a possible U.S. rate rise, some analysts and dealers said a tightening has already been factored in and that the dollar was looking overbought at current levels.

David Brown, economist at Bear Stearns in London, said the dollar was still subject to some short-term corrective losses. He noted that during the course of 1994, when the federal funds rate was doubled from 2.5 percent to 5.0 percent, dollar/mark crashed from 1.75 in February 1994 to 1.35 a year later.
